clue.text: Coren's crazy to be an editor

indicators.note: crazy means wild and mixed up, so these letters get rearranged

explanation.surface: Alan Coren, editor of Punch, is said to be mad to take the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crazy' signals an anagram of CORENS. Alan Coren was a British humorist and editor of Punch magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: A censor cuts and alters text before publication, a form of editing.

clue.text: What ambitious politicians aspire to — getting pissed with rotten Frost

parts.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, and drunk can be high
food that has gone off is rotten
frost is frozen ice crystals

explanation.surface: Politicians dream of power, or of getting drunk with the broadcaster David Frost.
explanation.walkthrough: Frost looks like Sir David Frost, the political interviewer, but it is just ice.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior post in government, such as a cabinet job, is what career politicians strive for.

clue.text: House material, but unable to take the blows, this MP?

definitions.text: House material, but unable to take the blows
definitions.meaning: first meaning: what the first little pig built his house of, blown down by the wolf
second meaning: Jack ..., Labour MP and frontbencher

explanation.walkthrough: 'House' looks like the House of Commons, but the first sense is the nursery tale of the three little pigs.
explanation.definitionFit: The material of the flimsiest pig's house shares its name with the Labour politician Jack Straw.

clue.text: Terrible peril of being an embryonic champion

indicators.note: terrible here means badly mangled, so the letters of peril of are reshuffled

explanation.surface: A dire warning about the risks run by a sporting champion still in the making.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible' signals an anagram of PERILOF. 'Embryonic champion' looks like a budding sports star; it means one who champions embryos.
explanation.definitionFit: Anti-abortion campaigners call their stance pro-life, defending the unborn foetus.

clue.text: Arevolting type of careless bloke's HIV

indicators.note: careless suggests things thrown together anyhow, so those letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A disgusting man who has caught HIV through carelessness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'careless' signals an anagram of BLOKESHIV. 'Revolting' means disgusting in the surface but rebellious in the definition; 'Arevolting' is a typo for 'A revolting'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Bolshevik was a Russian revolutionary, someone in revolt.

clue.text: Major, getting sod all right, upset boisterous party

indicators.note: upset means overturned, so in a down entry the letters are read from the bottom up

parts.note: John Major was Prime Minister, PM
sod all is British slang for nothing, which is O

explanation.surface: John Major, getting nothing right, overturns a rowdy gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: A romp is a lively, high-spirited frolic, a rowdy bit of fun.

clue.text: Rotten borough city once held back by clapped-out familiar Page 3 girl

indicators.note: held means kept within, so the ancient city goes inside the other letters

parts.note: something clapped-out is worn out and old
Sam Fox, a famous topless model in The Sun's Page 3, known familiarly as Sam

indicators.note: back means turned around, so the ancient city's name is read in reverse

parts.note: Ur was an ancient city of Mesopotamia

explanation.surface: Mockery of a constituency's sleaze, with a faded glamour model thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the ancient city into RU, and 'held' puts that inside the other pieces. Page 3 of The Sun printed topless photos; Samantha Fox, familiarly Sam, was its best-known model.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Sarum was the notorious rotten borough, an almost uninhabited place that still returned two MPs until 1832.

clue.text: Inside Rolls, round female takes Dick's thing -— thus are politicians' rewards revealed

parts.note: rolls are official lists of names, another word for which is a register
a round shape is the letter O
a dick is slang for the male member, so Dick's becomes member's
your thing is what you are into, your interests

explanation.surface: A smutty scene inside a Rolls-Royce, with a woman and a man called Dick, passed off as a revelation about politicians.
explanation.walkthrough: The register is the public record in which British MPs must declare paid work, gifts and shareholdings; Private Eye ran this in the cash-for-questions era of the mid-1990s.
explanation.definitionFit: The register is the published list where MPs declare outside payments and gifts, so it is where their rewards are made public.

clue.text: Luvwvie memoirist's a 'prick' in Old English

indicators.note: in tells us one piece sits inside the other, here the slang word placed within the abbreviation

parts.note: prick and tool are both slang for the penis

explanation.surface: A sneer at an actor's autobiography, calling its author a prick in old-fashioned language.
explanation.walkthrough: TOOL goes 'in' OE. Peter O'Toole, the actor, published memoirs (Loitering with Intent); luvvie is British slang for a theatrical type, and 'Luvwvie' is a typo for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter O'Toole was a flamboyant stage and screen actor, a classic luvvie, who wrote two volumes of autobiography.

clue.text: When one gets rotten maths it's a far from jolly wheeze

indicators.note: rotten means badly done, so the letters of maths are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: one is A, as in a single thing

explanation.surface: A student complains that bad maths marks leave them wheezing, and not in a fun way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rotten' turns MATHS into ASTHM, then 'one' adds A. A wheeze is also British slang for a jolly prank, hence 'far from jolly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Asthma is a lung condition whose typical symptom is wheezing, hardly a cheerful thing.

clue.text: It might mark a military departure — Mailer's final chance?

definitions.text: It might mark a military departure
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the bugle call played at military funerals and at the end of the day
second meaning: the last collection of the day, a sender's final chance to catch the mail

explanation.walkthrough: Mailer looks like the novelist Norman Mailer, but here it is just someone posting a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The bugle call sounded at soldiers' funerals shares its name with the day's final collection from a postbox.

clue.text: Abusing one's public position is bloody hard work!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: corruption, using office for personal gain
second meaning: British slang for strenuous toil

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that corruption, the first sense, is presented as if it were exhausting labour, the second.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both bribery and corrupt dealing in office and, in British slang, heavy physical labour.

clue.text: See 8
Complaint and catastrophe to which Major responded in a bull-headed way?

definitions.text: to which Major responded in a bull-headed way

parts.note: a beef is slang for a grievance
a crisis is an emergency or disaster

explanation.surface: John Major stubbornly mishandling a disaster, with a pun on bulls.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1996 the EU banned British beef over mad cow disease (BSE), and Major's government responded with a policy of non-co-operation in Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: The mad cow disease emergency of 1996 was met by the Major government with obstinate defiance, bull-headed in a cattle affair.

clue.text: Piss delicately on wicket causing a political scandal

parts.note: pass water is the polite way of saying piss
a wicket is a small gate

explanation.surface: A cricketer relieving himself on the pitch, causing an uproar.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'on' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nixon-era break-in and cover-up is the political scandal that gave every later one its '-gate' suffix.

clue.text: Here's a gem about Eggar — most satisfactory!

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the gem goes round the politician's name

parts.note: an opal is a gemstone
Tim Eggar was a Conservative minister in the 1990s

explanation.surface: Someone presents a jewel in honour of a minister and declares the result perfect.
explanation.definitionFit: Optimal describes the best possible outcome, the most favourable or satisfactory state.

clue.text: Scraps magazine associated with better times

parts.note: Punch was a British humour magazine
ups, as in ups and downs, are good times

explanation.surface: A magazine being thrown out, remembered from happier days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scraps' looks like waste or a verb meaning discards, but it is fights.
explanation.definitionFit: Scraps are fights or brawls, and so are punch-ups.

clue.text: Brian's ex left Kenneth's ex a hard choice

parts.note: DI, a woman's name, short for Diana
Emma Thompson was formerly married to the actor Kenneth Branagh

explanation.surface: Gossip-column tangle: one celebrity's former partner ditches another's former partner, leaving a tough decision.
explanation.definitionFit: A dilemma is a situation calling for a choice between two difficult or unwelcome options.

clue.text: Crack about unlikely MEP's onetime non-drinking

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the outer pair goes round the rest

parts.note: one gives A and time gives T, the standard abbreviation
TT, teetotal, is the abbreviation for someone who abstains from alcohol

indicators.note: unlikely suggests an improbable arrangement, so those letters are rearranged

parts.note: the three letters of Member of the European Parliament, the 's read as is

explanation.surface: A dry former Euro MP being cracked, an improbable sight.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a crack at something is to make a go or try at it.

clue.text: See 8
It's going back to Scotland you see direction on hated motorway feature

parts.note: S is south, one of the compass directions
traffic cones marking roadworks are a hated sight on British motorways

explanation.surface: A Scottish voice tells a driver which way to go past the much-loathed roadworks.
explanation.walkthrough: The Stone of Scone, taken to England in 1296, was returned to Scotland in 1996, the topical joke behind this definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stone of Scone, the coronation stone kept in Westminster Abbey, was being sent back north when this puzzle appeared.

clue.text: Awful military blazer

parts.note: blazer looks like a regimental jacket, but it is something that blazes: a dreadful incendiary weapon

explanation.walkthrough: A blazer is a jacket, often a regimental one, which is the misdirection; here it is something that burns.
explanation.definitionFit: The jellied petrol used in firebombs is a terrible weapon of war that sets everything alight.

clue.text: 'Up yours!': no street greeting, but oddly appropriate

indicators.note: no tells us these greeting letters are left out of the letters available
oddly means strangely, so what remains is jumbled

parts.note: yo is a slangy greeting heard on the street

explanation.surface: A rude gesture rather than a friendly hello, yet somehow fitting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no' removes YO from UPYOURS to leave UPURS, which 'oddly' rearranges. 'Appropriate' is a verb here (to take), not the adjective the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To usurp is to seize power or property without the right to it, to take it for oneself.

clue.text: Where justice is administered — Heseltine's first to be engulfed by attack of the sweats

indicators.note: engulfed by means swallowed up inside, so the single letter is placed within the illness

parts.note: the ague is a fever with fits of shivering and sweating, so an attack of it is the ague

indicators.note: first picks out just the opening letter of the minister's name

parts.note: the first letter of Heseltine, the Conservative Deputy Prime Minister

explanation.surface: Michael Heseltine, a senior Conservative, breaking into a nervous sweat.
explanation.walkthrough: THE AGUE is 'to be engulfed by' H, the first letter of Heseltine; 'the' does double duty in the surface and the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dutch city is home to the International Court of Justice and other international tribunals.

clue.text: Pig, it's said, who's responsible for knocking off cows

definitions.text: who's responsible for knocking off cows

indicators.note: it's said means when spoken aloud, so the word for pig sounds the same as the name

parts.note: a hog is a pig

explanation.surface: An insult hurled at the man overseeing the slaughter of cattle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's said' makes HOG a sound-alike for the surname. Douglas Hogg was Minister of Agriculture during the 1996 mad cow (BSE) crisis, when infected herds were culled.
explanation.definitionFit: As Agriculture Minister he directed the mass cull of cattle during the BSE outbreak.

clue.text: Interest taken by politician in broadcaster is very revealing

indicators.note: in places the combined pieces inside the name of the broadcaster

parts.note: Sky is a British satellite broadcaster

indicators.note: taken by says the letter for interest goes along with the politician, side by side

parts.note: I is the standard abbreviation for interest in finance
MP, Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician with a financial stake in a TV company, an exposé of the kind Private Eye loves.
explanation.definitionFit: Skimpy clothing covers little of the body, so it shows a lot.

clue.text: Piss artist about to consume a vast quantity gets plug

indicators.note: about means around, so the drunkard's word surrounds the greedy eating

parts.note: a piss artist is British slang for a drunk, a sot
to pig is to eat greedily, to pig out

explanation.surface: A drunk about to down an enormous amount, then getting thumped.
explanation.walkthrough: SOT goes 'about' PIG. 'Plug' looks like a punch here, but it is the stopper for a cask.
explanation.definitionFit: A spigot is a peg or plug used to stop the vent hole in a cask, or a tap.

clue.text: Service accommodation salesman in stupor till October

indicators.note: in shows that the letters sit inside the run of words stupor till October

parts.note: the letters run from the end of stupor through till into the first letter of October, spelling the minister's surname

explanation.surface: A salesman lying dazed until autumn, as if Parliament's long summer recess.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Portillo, Defence Secretary in 1996, sold the armed forces' married quarters housing to a private company.
explanation.definitionFit: As Defence Secretary he oversaw the sale of the Ministry of Defence's service family housing, so he sold off service homes.
